If we let $u=4x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi /8$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}5\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

If we let $u=4 x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,\Longrightarrow\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sin{\left(4 x \right)}\,\text{d}x &= 1\int \sin(u)\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\ &= \frac{1}{4}\int \sin(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &= - \frac{\cos{\left(u \right)}}{4}+C \\ &= - \frac{\cos{\left(4 x \right)}}{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=3 - 18 x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-18\,\Longrightarrow\,\text{d}x=- \frac{1}{18}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \cos{\left(18 x - 3 \right)}\,\text{d}x &= 1\int \cos(u)\cdot - \frac{1}{18}\,\text{d}u \\ &= - \frac{1}{18}\int \cos(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &= - \frac{\sin{\left(u \right)}}{18}+C \\ &= \frac{\sin{\left(18 x - 3 \right)}}{18}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=4 x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,\Longrightarrow\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{8}}9 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}\,\text{d}x &= {\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}9\sin(u)\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\ &= \frac{9}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sin(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &= - \frac{9 \cos{\left(u \right)}}{4}\big|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= 0-(- \frac{9}{4}) \\ &= \frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=\frac{\pi x}{2},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\pi}{2}\,\Longrightarrow\,\text{d}x=\frac{2}{\pi}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\cos{\left(\frac{\pi x}{2} \right)}\,\text{d}x &= {\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}1\cos(u)\cdot \frac{2}{\pi}\,\text{d}u \\ &= \frac{2}{\pi}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cos(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &= \frac{2 \sin{\left(u \right)}}{\pi}\big|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \frac{2}{\pi}-(0) \\ &= \frac{2}{\pi}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=6 x + \frac{\pi}{3},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,\Longrightarrow\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{18}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{2 \pi}{3}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{18}}\sin{\left(6 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\,\text{d}x &= {\int }_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}}1\sin(u)\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\ &= \frac{1}{6}{\int }_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}}\sin(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &= - \frac{\cos{\left(u \right)}}{6}\big|_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}} \\ &= \frac{1}{12}-(- \frac{1}{12}) \\ &= \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$
